about: Chemical Library for The Virtual Neuro Lab. Each entry says what the substance is and what it does in a REAL fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster), in plain words, with the fly molecules it acts on and the papers behind it. No simulation results or verdicts live here - those belong to the experiments part of the lab.

fly.label: Shown in fruit flies
fly.help: The effect or target was demonstrated in Drosophila.

insect.label: Shown in other insects
insect.help: Shown in mosquitoes, cockroaches or other insects; assumed, not proven, for fruit flies.

mammal.label: Borrowed from mammals
mammal.help: Known from mammal studies; the fly version is a reasonable guess, not a finding.

none.label: No fly target known
none.help: Flies lack the molecule this acts on in people, or nothing is known.

chemicals.name: Caffeine
chemicals.what: The stimulant in coffee, tea and energy drinks.
chemicals.fly: Flies given caffeine sleep less, especially at night. Surprisingly, this does not need the fly's adenosine receptor (caffeine's main target in people). It needs PKA (a cAMP-driven signalling enzyme) and dopamine made by a cluster of brain cells called the PAM neurons. Flies also taste caffeine as bitter and avoid eating it.
chemicals.route: Eaten (mixed into food); tasted on the legs and mouthparts.

targets.name: Gr66a, Gr33a, Gr93a
targets.role: bitter taste receptors that detect caffeine

targets.name: AdoR
targets.role: the fly's only adenosine receptor - not needed for the sleep effect

refs.claim: caffeine promotes wakefulness via dopamine and PAM neurons, independently of the adenosine receptor
caffeine's effect on fly sleep requires PKA activity but not the adenosine receptor
Gr66a is required for the caffeine taste response
several gustatory receptors, including Gr93a, are needed to detect caffeine

chemicals.name: Theophylline
chemicals.what: A caffeine relative used as an asthma medicine; tea contains only trace amounts.
chemicals.fly: No fruit-fly study is on file. In people it blocks adenosine receptors (more strongly than caffeine) and, at higher doses, the enzyme that breaks down cAMP. Because caffeine's wake effect in flies runs through cAMP and dopamine rather than the adenosine receptor, the mammal ranking may not carry over to flies.

targets.name: unknown in flies
targets.role: adenosine receptors and phosphodiesterase in mammals

refs.claim: adenosine-receptor potency theophylline > caffeine > theobromine (mammalian)

chemicals.name: Theobromine
chemicals.what: The caffeine relative in chocolate and cocoa.
chemicals.fly: No fruit-fly study is on file. In people it is a weaker adenosine blocker than caffeine. As with theophylline, the mammal ranking may not carry over to flies, because caffeine works in flies through cAMP and dopamine instead.

refs.claim: adenosine-receptor potency theophylline > caffeine > theobromine (mammalian)

chemicals.name: Nicotine
chemicals.what: The addictive chemical in tobacco. Plants make it as a natural insecticide.
chemicals.fly: Nicotine switches on nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, which carry most of the fast 'go' signals between nerve cells in the fly brain. Flies exposed to nicotine vapour first become hyperactive, then uncoordinated, and at higher doses stop moving. The fly's dopamine system shapes how strongly it reacts.
chemicals.route: Breathed in as vapour, or eaten.

targets.name: nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
targets.role: the fly brain's main fast excitatory receptors

refs.claim: dopamine modulates acute responses to cocaine, nicotine and ethanol in Drosophila

chemicals.name: Imidacloprid
chemicals.what: A neonicotinoid insecticide, widely used on crops.
chemicals.fly: It grips the same nicotinic acetylcholine receptors as nicotine, but far more tightly in insects than in mammals, which is what makes it an insecticide. Low doses disturb movement and behaviour; high doses cause paralysis and death.

targets.name: nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
targets.role: binds them very tightly in insects

refs.claim: imidacloprid binds acetylcholine receptors from Drosophila heads

chemicals.name: Aldicarb
chemicals.what: A carbamate insecticide, now heavily restricted.
chemicals.fly: It blocks acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that clears acetylcholine away after each signal. Acetylcholine piles up, nerve cells are over-stimulated, and the fly goes from tremors and loss of coordination to paralysis and death. It is a poison, not a stimulant.

refs.claim: engineered Drosophila acetylcholinesterase used to detect organophosphate and carbamate pesticides

chemicals.name: Muscarine
chemicals.what: A mushroom toxin found in Inocybe and Clitocybe mushrooms. It was first isolated from the fly agaric, which contains only traces.
chemicals.fly: It switches on muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, mainly the A-type. In flies these are slow 'tuning' receptors, not the main fast signal; the A-type, for example, works in the mushroom body during learning. So muscarine should change how circuits are tuned rather than simply turning brain activity up. (Receptor responses were measured on fly receptors grown in cultured cells.)

refs.cite: Collin et al. (2013) Cell Mol Life Sci 70:3231
refs.claim: muscarine strongly activates the fly A-type muscarinic receptor; the B-type is far less sensitive (tested in cultured cells)
muscarinic receptor mAChR-A in mushroom-body neurons is needed for aversive olfactory learning

chemicals.name: Atropine
chemicals.what: A drug from deadly nightshade, used by doctors to widen pupils and speed up the heart.
chemicals.fly: It blocks muscarinic receptors. Flies have three types: the A-type is blocked by atropine, the B-type is not, and the C-type has not been tested. It does not block the fast nicotinic signals that carry most of the traffic in the fly brain.

refs.cite: Collin et al. (2013) Cell Mol Life Sci 70:3231
refs.claim: Drosophila has A- and B-type muscarinic receptors; classic blockers such as atropine and scopolamine block the A-type but not the B-type

chemicals.name: Scopolamine
chemicals.what: A nightshade-plant drug used against motion sickness.
chemicals.fly: Like atropine, it blocks the fly's A-type muscarinic receptor but not the B-type (the C-type is untested), and leaves the fast nicotinic signals alone.

refs.cite: Collin et al. (2013) Cell Mol Life Sci 70:3231
refs.claim: Drosophila has A- and B-type muscarinic receptors; classic blockers such as atropine and scopolamine block the A-type but not the B-type

chemicals.name: Picrotoxin
chemicals.what: A plant poison that causes convulsions.
chemicals.fly: It blocks the fly's main 'brake' receptor, the GABA-gated chloride channel called Rdl. In flies it also blocks glutamate-gated chloride channels, because glutamate acts as a calming signal in parts of the fly brain. So it removes two brakes at once. A single change in Rdl makes flies resistant to it and to some insecticides.
chemicals.route: Eaten, or applied to the brain in recordings.

refs.claim: a point mutation in the Drosophila Rdl GABA receptor confers resistance to picrotoxin and dieldrin
glutamate is an inhibitory transmitter in the fly olfactory system via GluClα, blocked by picrotoxin

chemicals.sci: an equal mixture of picrotoxinin (C15H16O6) and picrotin (C15H18O7)

chemicals.name: Pentylenetetrazole (PTZ)
chemicals.what: A drug used in labs to trigger seizures.
chemicals.fly: In mammals it blocks GABA-A 'brake' receptors. Flies fed it are used as a seizure and brain-plasticity model, though its exact target in the fly is less well defined.

targets.name: Rdl (probable)
targets.role: GABA receptor, by analogy with mammals

refs.cite: Mohammad, Singh & Sharma (2009) BMC Syst Biol 3:11
refs.claim: Drosophila PTZ feeding model of seizure-related plasticity

chemicals.name: Phenobarbital
chemicals.what: An old sleep and anti-seizure medicine (a barbiturate).
chemicals.fly: In mammals it strengthens the GABA 'brake'. In flies it is best known for something else, shown directly in flies: it switches on detox genes (cytochrome P450s) through the CncC pathway. Its sedating effect in flies is borrowed from mammal studies.

targets.name: CncC / Maf-S
targets.role: switches on detox genes (shown in flies)

refs.claim: CncC/Maf drives the fly's transcriptional response to phenobarbital

chemicals.name: Vigabatrin
chemicals.what: An epilepsy medicine.
chemicals.fly: It permanently blocks GABA transaminase, the enzyme that breaks GABA down, so GABA builds up. Flies have the same enzyme (Gabat); flies missing it have two to three times more brain GABA and sleep more, the best clue to what the drug would do. Recovery needs new enzyme, which takes days.

refs.claim: vigabatrin irreversibly inhibits GABA transaminase (mammalian review)
flies lacking GABA transaminase have raised brain GABA and more sleep

chemicals.name: Isoflurane
chemicals.what: A gas anaesthetic used in surgery.
chemicals.fly: Flies breathing it are knocked out and recover once it is removed. Fly genetics has shown that the brain's sleep–wake circuits change how sensitive a fly is to it.

targets.name: several
targets.role: no single target; sleep–wake circuits set sensitivity

refs.claim: a sleep/wake circuit controls isoflurane sensitivity in Drosophila

chemicals.name: Ethanol
chemicals.what: Drinking alcohol.
chemicals.fly: Flies respond much like people: a short burst of hyperactivity, then loss of coordination, then sedation. With repeated exposure they become tolerant, and they can come to prefer alcohol-laced food.
chemicals.route: Breathed in as vapour, or eaten.

targets.name: several
targets.role: GABA receptors, dopamine signalling and more

refs.claim: ethanol first stimulates then sedates Drosophila locomotion
flies come to prefer ethanol-containing food, with features of addiction

chemicals.name: Tetrodotoxin (TTX)
chemicals.what: The pufferfish poison.
chemicals.fly: It plugs voltage-gated sodium channels. In flies that channel is made by the para gene. Without it, nerve cells cannot fire, and the result is paralysis. Fly labs use it to silence nerve signals during recordings.

refs.cite: Warmke et al. (1997) J Gen Physiol 110:119
refs.claim: the Drosophila para sodium channel, expressed in oocytes, is blocked by tetrodotoxin

chemicals.sci: a guanidinium alkaloid (aminoperhydroquinazoline) from the bacteria that live in pufferfish

chemicals.name: Tetanus toxin
chemicals.what: The bacterial toxin behind tetanus (lockjaw).
chemicals.fly: It cuts synaptobrevin, a protein nerve cells need to release their signals. In flies it is not fed: researchers make chosen nerve cells produce it, as a genetic tool to switch those cells' outputs off. The cells still fire, but no chemical signal reaches the next cell.

refs.claim: targeted tetanus-toxin light chain blocks synaptic transmission in Drosophila

chemicals.sci: tetanospasmin, a zinc protease made by the bacterium Clostridium tetani

chemicals.name: Permethrin
chemicals.what: A pyrethroid insecticide used on clothing, pets and crops.
chemicals.fly: It holds the para sodium channel open, so nerve cells fire over and over. Flies show 'knockdown' (twitching and falling over), then paralysis. Changes in the para gene, the 'kdr' mutations, make flies resistant.

targets.name: para
targets.role: the sodium channel it holds open

refs.claim: pyrethroids act on insect sodium channels

refs.cite: Pittendrigh et al. (1997) Mol Gen Genet 256:602
refs.claim: para sodium-channel mutations give pyrethroid resistance in Drosophila

chemicals.name: Paraquat
chemicals.formula: C12H14N2²⁺ (sold as the dichloride salt, C12H14Cl2N2)
chemicals.what: A weed-killer, banned in many countries.
chemicals.fly: It produces damaging reactive oxygen inside cells. Flies fed paraquat develop movement problems and die early, so it is widely used as an oxidative-stress test and a Parkinson's-like model. Some labs report the loss of particular dopamine neurons; others do not see it.

targets.name: dopamine neurons
targets.role: reported as especially vulnerable in some studies

refs.claim: paraquat causes dopamine-neuron loss and parkinsonian symptoms in Drosophila
no dopamine-neuron loss found in several fly Parkinson's models, paraquat included

chemicals.name: Amphetamine
chemicals.what: A stimulant medicine.
chemicals.fly: It works through the fly's dopamine transporter (DAT). It runs the transporter backwards, so dopamine leaks out of nerve endings, and flies become more active. Fly larvae lacking DAT don't speed up on it.

refs.claim: amphetamine's effect on movement needs the dopamine transporter (shown in fly larvae)
amphetamine's effect on dopamine vesicles observed in the Drosophila brain

chemicals.name: Cocaine
chemicals.what: A stimulant from coca leaves.
chemicals.fly: It blocks the dopamine transporter, so dopamine lingers at the cells that receive it. Flies show a dose-dependent sequence: extra grooming, then hyperactivity and circling, and at high doses they stop moving altogether. Repeat doses make them more sensitive.
chemicals.route: Breathed in as vapour (free-base), or eaten.

refs.claim: stereotyped, dose-dependent cocaine behaviours and sensitisation in Drosophila
dopamine modulates acute cocaine responses in Drosophila

chemicals.name: Bupropion
chemicals.what: An antidepressant and quit-smoking medicine.
chemicals.fly: In people it slows the clearing of dopamine and noradrenaline and weakly blocks nicotinic receptors. Flies have a dopamine transporter it could act on, but no noradrenaline; octopamine plays that role. No direct fruit-fly study is on file.

targets.name: DAT (probable)
targets.role: dopamine transporter, by analogy with mammals

refs.cite: Stahl et al. (2004) Prim Care Companion J Clin Psychiatry 6:159
refs.claim: bupropion inhibits dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake (mammalian)

refs.cite: Slemmer, Martin & Damaj (2000) J Pharmacol Exp Ther 295:321
refs.claim: bupropion blocks nicotinic receptors (mammalian)

chemicals.name: Dopamine
chemicals.what: One of the fly's own brain signals, for reward, punishment and wakefulness.
chemicals.fly: Different dopamine neurons signal reward or punishment for learning, and dopamine keeps flies awake. What it does depends on the receiving receptor: Dop1R1 and Dop1R2 generally excite, Dop2R calms, and DopEcR also responds to a steroid hormone. To raise brain dopamine, researchers usually feed its building block, L-DOPA, rather than dopamine itself.
chemicals.route: Made in the brain; raised experimentally by feeding L-DOPA.

refs.claim: review of Drosophila dopamine genes, receptors, drugs and behaviours
dopamine controls arousal and sleep in Drosophila (DAT mutant fumin)

chemicals.name: Octopamine
chemicals.what: The fly's own 'fight-or-flight' signal, its version of noradrenaline.
chemicals.fly: It raises arousal, activity and energy use, and is needed for normal flight, egg-laying and aggression. It acts on several receptors and also travels in the blood as a hormone.
chemicals.route: Made in the brain; released into synapses and the blood.

refs.claim: octopamine as the insect arousal amine and hormone

chemicals.name: DEET
chemicals.what: The most common insect repellent.
chemicals.fly: Flies avoid DEET mainly by taste. It switches on avoidance (bitter) taste neurons through the receptors Gr32a, Gr33a and Gr66a, and flies with no sense of smell still refuse DEET-laced food. DEET also acts on smell neurons, but exactly how is still debated.

targets.name: Gr32a, Gr33a, Gr66a
targets.role: avoidance taste receptors that DEET switches on

targets.name: Orco
targets.role: smell co-receptor; DEET's effect here is debated

refs.claim: DEET activates avoidance taste neurons via Gr32a, Gr33a and Gr66a; smell is not required
DEET inhibits Orco-dependent odour responses (later debated)
Ir40a proposed as a DEET-sensing olfactory receptor (later disputed)

chemicals.name: Picaridin
chemicals.what: A modern insect repellent.
chemicals.fly: Mosquito studies show it changes how smell receptors respond. No direct fruit-fly study is on file.

refs.claim: picaridin and DEET modulate mosquito odorant receptors

chemicals.name: Citronellal
chemicals.what: The lemony smell in citronella and lemongrass oil.
chemicals.fly: Flies avoid its smell. That avoidance needs both the smell co-receptor Orco and the TRPA1 channel in smell neurons.

refs.claim: fly TRPA1 in smell neurons is required to avoid citronellal

chemicals.name: PMD (oil of lemon eucalyptus)
chemicals.what: The active ingredient of refined oil of lemon eucalyptus repellents.
chemicals.fly: Mosquitoes smell it and avoid it, and it triggers responses in their smell neurons. Fruit-fly studies are thin.

refs.claim: PMD repels three mosquito species and triggers olfactory nerve responses

chemicals.name: Cinnamaldehyde
chemicals.what: The flavour and smell of cinnamon.
chemicals.fly: In mammals cinnamaldehyde switches on TRPA1, an irritant-sensing channel. Flies have TRPA1 in their bitter taste neurons, where it senses reactive irritants like this one, so flies probably taste it as unpleasant. A fly test of cinnamaldehyde itself is not on file.

targets.name: TRPA1
targets.role: irritant channel in bitter taste neurons (expected target)

refs.claim: cinnamaldehyde activates mammalian TRPA1
fly TRPA1 in taste neurons senses reactive irritants

chemicals.name: Camphor
chemicals.what: The strong cooling smell in vapour rubs.
chemicals.fly: In mammals it activates TRPV1 and blocks TRPA1. Flies can smell it, but direct fly studies of how it acts are thin.

refs.claim: camphor activates TRPV1 and inhibits TRPA1 (mammalian)

chemicals.name: Piperine
chemicals.what: The hot compound in black pepper.
chemicals.fly: In mammals it activates the TRPV1 and TRPA1 'spice' channels. Flies have no direct match for mammalian TRPV1, so its fly target is unknown.

refs.claim: review: piperine activates TRPV1 and TRPA1 (mammalian)

chemicals.name: Eugenol
chemicals.what: The smell of cloves.
chemicals.fly: Studies in cockroaches and ants, and on insect receptors grown in cultured cells, suggest it acts on octopamine receptors. This has not been shown in living fruit flies, which mainly meet it as a smell.

refs.claim: eugenol acts via octopamine receptors in insects

chemicals.name: Limonene
chemicals.what: The main smell in orange and lemon peel.
chemicals.fly: Flies smell it through Or19a smell neurons, which respond to citrus smells (most strongly valencene, and also limonene) and help females choose citrus fruit for laying eggs. Claims that limonene blocks acetylcholinesterase come from weak effects in grain pests, not flies.

targets.name: Or19a
targets.role: citrus smell receptor (valencene first, limonene too)

refs.claim: Or19a neurons respond to citrus terpenes (valencene, limonene) and guide egg-laying on citrus

chemicals.name: Sucrose
chemicals.what: Table sugar.
chemicals.fly: Sweet taste neurons on the legs and mouthparts detect it through the Gr5a and Gr64 receptor family. Flies find it attractive, and it is food.

refs.claim: two Gr genes underlie sugar reception in Drosophila

chemicals.name: Sodium chloride
chemicals.what: Table salt.
chemicals.fly: Low salt is attractive and high salt is avoided. Low salt is sensed by sweet taste cells using the receptor Ir56b with the helper receptors Ir25a and Ir76b. High salt is sensed by bitter cells and by dedicated high-salt cells that use Ir7c (with the same helpers).

refs.claim: Ir76b mediates attraction to low salt in Drosophila
high-salt avoidance circuits in Drosophila
Ir7c is a high-salt receptor working with Ir25a and Ir76b
Ir56b underlies the attractive low-salt response in Drosophila

chemicals.name: Melatonin
chemicals.what: The 'night hormone' in people, sold as a sleep aid.
chemicals.fly: Insects make melatonin, but its role in fruit flies is unclear and no fly melatonin receptor has been identified.

refs.claim: insects make melatonin via the vertebrate serotonin pathway (mini-review)

chemicals.name: Morphine
chemicals.what: A strong painkiller from the opium poppy.
chemicals.fly: Flies don't have the opioid receptors morphine acts on in people (their nearest relatives are allatostatin-C receptors), so there is no known direct target in the fly. Small effects on fly behaviour have been reported, but not through that route.
